title: Base rates in conditional probability
learning_objectives: Use natural frequencies to combine prevalence, sensitivity, and false-positive rate.
Distinguish P(positive | condition) from P(condition | positive).
Explain why a rare condition can produce many false positives.

misconceptions.description: A test with 90% sensitivity means a positive result gives a 90% probability of the condition.
The prevalence of the condition does not affect the meaning of a positive result.

critical_errors.description: Reverses P(positive | condition) and P(condition | positive).
Calculates a posterior probability while omitting the base rate.

teaching_brief.goal: Help the learner reason from a population table rather than reverse a conditional probability.
teaching_brief.learner_profile: A learner comfortable with percentages but new to Bayes' rule.
instructions: Start with a hypothetical population of 1,000 or 10,000 people.
Separate true positives from false positives.
Ask the learner to identify the denominator for P(condition | positive).
Check understanding with a new prevalence.
prohibited_disclosures: Do not reveal held-out item wording.
Do not equate sensitivity with positive predictive value.

pretest.prompt: A condition affects 1% of people. A test finds 90% of affected people and is positive for 10% of unaffected people. Why can most positive results be false positives?

choices.text: The unaffected population is much larger.
A positive test always means no condition.

posttest.prompt: Among 1,000 people, 10 have a condition. A test correctly flags 9 of them and falsely flags 99 others. What fraction of all positive results are true positives?
To calculate P(condition | positive), what should be in the denominator of a natural-frequency calculation?

choices.text: All positive results, true and false

transfer.prompt: The same test is used in a high-risk clinic where prevalence is much higher. With sensitivity and specificity unchanged, what generally happens to P(condition | positive)?

choices.text: It becomes equal to sensitivity by definition.

transfer.prompt: In 100 items, 20 are defective. A detector flags 18 defective and 8 nondefective items. What fraction of flagged items are actually defective?

retention.prompt: A highly accurate detector is applied to an extremely rare event. Which information remains essential for interpreting an alert?
Why are natural frequencies useful in Bayes problems?

choices.text: They make the relevant groups and denominator visible.
They guarantee a positive result is correct.
They replace the need for base rates.
